stem: An experiment records inputs $[1,2,3,4,5]$ and outputs $[5.200000, 12.895079, 23.677684, 34.622023, 47.691348]$. Fit a straight line to $(\ln x,\ln y)$; use the displayed outputs as the data. Unless otherwise stated, give numerical answers exactly or to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the log-linear regression equation and hence the power model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the sum of squared residuals on the original output scale.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the output at input 3.5 and at input 20.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the two predictions warrant different confidence and why log-scale least squares is a modelling choice.

steps.text: Transform every positive input and output using natural logarithms.

Subtract each prediction from the observed output and square.

That choice gives a relative-error interpretation and should be checked against the experiment.

subject: math-ai-hl
title: Uncertain saturation inversion
stem: A sensor output is $S(x)=100x/(4+x)$ for concentration $x\geq0$. A reading of 60 has uncertainty $\pm1$ output unit. Unless otherwise stated, give numerical answers exactly or to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the range and find the inverse.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the concentration estimate and the interval allowed by the uncertain reading.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the concentrations at outputs 90% and 95% of capacity.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain a measurement concern near saturation.

steps.text: Multiply out $S(K+x)=Lx$ and collect the terms in $x$.
The inverse is increasing, so invert endpoints 59 and 61.
A five percentage point output increase more than doubles this concentration.
The inverse becomes very steep as the reading approaches the capacity.
Small output uncertainty then produces a large concentration uncertainty.

subject: math-ai-hl
title: Delayed seasonal demand
stem: An old demand model is $f(t)=25+7\cos(\pi t/6)$. A changed season is modelled by $g(t)=f(t-0.4)+2$, with $0\leq t\leq12$. Unless otherwise stated, give numerical answers exactly or to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the changes and state the new range.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the time of maximum demand and the new demand at month 6.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A planner instead uses $f(t)+2$ at month 6. Calculate the prediction error and explain its cause.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how observations could test the two changes separately.

steps.text: The demand pattern is delayed by 0.4 months.
The baseline is increased by 2 units.
Subtract the planner prediction from the shifted-model prediction.
The planner adjusts the baseline but ignores the timing change.
Timing of peaks and troughs tests the horizontal shift.
The midpoint between maximum and minimum tests the changed baseline.
Several cycles are preferable because one unusual season can distort either estimate.

subject: math-ai-hl
title: Changing a production regime
stem: A production total is $P(t)=5t$ for $0\leq t<3$, then $P(t)=L-20e^{-k(t-3)}$ for $t\geq3$. The join is continuous. Immediately after the join the rate of increase is 2 units per day. Unless otherwise stated, give numerical answers exactly or to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find $L$ using continuity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the given rate to find $k$. The derivative of the second formula is $20ke^{-k(t-3)}$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find when the total reaches 30 units.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State the long-term total and assess whether the join describes a smooth change of rate.

steps.text: The left rate is 5, whereas the right rate is 2.
The values join continuously but the rates differ, representing an abrupt regime change.
A gradual transition would require a different joining function or additional data.
